While I don't necessarily agree with this decision, I have to say, the shop owners were obviously irresponsible and had no concern over who they were selling firearms too. Every shop owner I know (and every shop I've worked at) has always opted to error on the side of caution when it comes to questionable purchasers.

The reason there isn't anything more concrete in place with regards to straw purchase prevention law is that the prevailing wisdom is store owners will decline a sale if they suspect anything is wrong. One of the stores I worked at had a string of a half dozen very specific models of handguns (highpoint, if anyone is curious) show up in shootings over the course of a month or so, all traced back to our store. From that point on, the owner instructed us to deny sales of that particular model to certain a certain demographic of customer. We didn't have any issues from that point on.

There is no law that requires a firearms dealer to sell you anything. If he doesn't like your brand of shoes, the way you talk to his staff, the attitude you have, anything, they can deny the sale regardless of your ability to pass a background check. It sounds to me like these dealers were far more concerned with making the sale than being responsible FFL holders.
